title: How To Prevent Covid From Creating A ‘Lost Generation Of Students’
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Wexler reports evidence that remote schooling has hurt vulnerable students most, citing McKinsey projections, Zearn usage data and rising course failures in Maryland. She argues the usual remedies of more money, tutoring and after-school programmes have a limited record, and she rejects proposals to downplay phonics. Her central claim is that reading comprehension depends on topic knowledge rather than on generic skills such as finding the main idea, so schools should adopt topic-organised, content-rich elementary literacy curricula. Wealthier children pick up academic knowledge and vocabulary at home, which helps explain the achievement gap. For older students she recommends content tutoring and explicit sentence-level writing instruction to compensate for knowledge gaps.
points: Remote learning losses fall hardest on Black, Hispanic, low-income, disabled and English-learner students, and the apparent reading bright spot likely misses disadvantaged children.
Reading comprehension depends more on knowledge of the topic than on practising transferable skills such as finding the main idea.
Content-rich, topic-organised literacy curricula are available, no costlier than skills-based ones, and a practical starting point for narrowing gaps.
Wealthier students absorb academic knowledge and vocabulary at home, which explains part of the achievement gap.
For older students, content-focused tutoring and explicit writing instruction from the sentence level can compensate for missing knowledge.
quotes: Back in the spring, experts predicted that the switch to remote learning would have a serious negative impact, especially on students who are Black, Hispanic, diagnosed with disabilities, learning English, or who come from low-income families. We now know those dire predictions were largely on target, leading a former secretary of education to express concern about “a lost generation of students.

Another study drew on data from a digital math platform called Zearn, which was serving approximately 925,000 students in kindergarten through fifth grade before the pandemic. The study found a huge socioeconomic divergence that hadn’t existed previously: kids from wealthier families were doing more math than before, while those from poor families were doing less.
Well-intentioned as they are, proposals like that can do more harm than good. Kids do need time to play, and they can acquire scientific knowledge from nature.
The vast majority of schools teach reading comprehension as a set of skills: finding the main idea, making inferences, etc. Those skills are what reading tests purport to measure.

Kids from more highly educated families—who are generally also wealthier—are able to pick up academic knowledge and vocabulary at home, whether or not they acquire it at school. That gives them a better chance of understanding the passages on reading tests, which aren’t tied to the content of the school curriculum.

We now have readily available elementary literacy curricula that are organized by topic rather than “skill,” and that cover meaty subjects in history, science, and the arts as well as literature. They cost no more than the old “skills”-focused curricula that haven’t worked, and some of them are even available for free.
A more realistic approach is to use explicit writing instruction, beginning at the sentence level, to build knowledge and compensate for gaps.
